title: Augments & Ink — Unlicensed Installation and Tattoo Clinic, Rogers Park Gray Zone
body:
# Augments & Ink — Unlicensed Installation and Tattoo Clinic, Rogers Park Gray Zone

**Location:** 6114 North Clark Street, Rogers Park Gray Zone, Zone 3. Ground floor of a four-story mixed residential building. Exterior: red door, iron security grate painted over several times, a sign that says AUGMENTS & INK in hand-cut vinyl lettering, and beneath it in smaller text: *Walk-ins welcome. Installations by appointment. No corponation IDs required or accepted.*

## The Shop

The front room is the tattoo parlor. Flash art covers every wall — not prints, original designs, most of them done by the shop's operator and some by clients who paid in artwork because they couldn't pay any other way. There are two tattoo stations: one in use, one for overflow when there's a second artist. A glass display case holds jewelry: steel, titanium, and a small locked section of subdermal pieces that aren't technically jewelry at all. A couch, worn to the shape of whoever sits in it most. A kettle. A playlist that hasn't been updated in six years because the current one is perfect.

The back room is through a door that has a curtain over it. Most clients never go through the curtain. The ones who do don't describe it the same way twice, which is partly because the rig looks different depending on what they were expecting and partly because they were usually scared.

## The Installer

**Thessaly Bowen-Nakamura**, 47, runs the shop alone except when she doesn't.

She was a field technician for Ferrogate Transit for eleven years — the person who went out to relay stations when the automated diagnostic systems found something the automated repair systems couldn't fix. That work teaches you that most problems are simpler than they look, and that machines fail in predictable ways if you understand the design, and that design files are the closest thing to a map of anything that exists. She left Ferrogate in circumstances that her NDA prevents her from describing. She bought the shop six months later.

The rig in the back came first, actually. She acquired it from a Ferrogate freight manifest error — a crate that showed up at a relay station scheduled for demolition, addressed to a subsidiary that had been dissolved two years prior. She signed for it. No one came to collect it. Six months after she left Ferrogate, she had figured out what every component did. Six months after that, she did her first installation on herself: a secondhand proprioceptive feedback loop in her left forearm that she'd reprinted from a pirated Ringo design file. It worked. The scar is visible if you know where to look.

She does the tattooing. The rig does the installation. She configures the rig, monitors the process, troubleshoots when it goes wrong, and talks clients through what's happening because most people who go under the rig are less afraid of the machine than of being alone with a machine they don't understand while their body is doing something irreversible.

She is not warm, exactly. She is precise. The precision reads as care in the right light.

## The Rig

No one calls it anything. It is the rig.

The installation bay occupies most of the back room. At the center is a medical-grade recline table, the kind that adjusts into configurations a standard chair cannot. It is old — the padding is real vinyl, cracked and repaired with adhesive tape in two places — but the hydraulics work and the positioning is accurate to two millimeters, which is what matters. Above the table, mounted to a ceiling rail: three articulated arms, each approximately 90 centimeters when extended, each ending in a tool cluster that can swap configurations in under four seconds. The arms were industrial welding units in their previous life. The end effectors are not. The end effectors are Thessaly's own design, printed and reprinted over six years of incremental refinement, and she will not discuss where she sources the materials for the fine-tolerance cutting and threading tools.

The manacles are bolted to the table rails. They are padded with silicone sleeves, the kind used in physical therapy. They close over wrists, ankles, and sometimes the neck depending on the installation site, with a quarter-turn latch that can be opened from inside by the patient if they can reach it, which during an active installation they usually cannot. This is not cruelty. This is physics: the rig performs cutting and threading operations at tolerances measured in microns, and a flinch — even a small one, even an involuntary one in response to something that isn't pain yet — is measured in millimeters. The manacles keep the work site still. The rig does the rest.

Five screens. One displays the installation design file: the component, the interface points, the routing for neural threading and SNT application, the expected tissue response at each stage. One displays patient vitals: heart rate, blood oxygen, dermal conductance, and a proprietary stress index that Thessaly calculated herself based on six years of observation and that she has never written down anywhere. Two are rig monitoring: arm positioning, tool status, SNT tank pressure and temperature, the live camera feeds from the work-site optics. The fifth screen is for music, because silence makes the sounds the rig makes harder to ignore.

Two glass tanks on the left wall contain SNT — Synthetic Neural Terminus — a milky, faintly blue-tinged solution when properly mixed, kept at 38.2 degrees Celsius, which is one degree above body temperature and the point at which the engineered protein matrix becomes receptive to neural tissue. The tanks have a pressure system. During bonding, SNT is delivered to the work site at 0.3 atmospheres through a needle no wider than a human hair. When it is working correctly it smells like burnt copper. When it is not working correctly, the smell changes. Thessaly has learned every variant of the smell.

Above the table: three camera clusters, each the size of a fist, each with six lenses at different magnifications. The rig sees the work site better than human eyes can. This is the point.

## The Installation Process

**Consultation:** Clients book in person, because Thessaly does not keep digital appointment records. The consultation happens at the tattoo counter, in the front room, with the kettle on. She asks what they want, where they want it, what they're hoping it will do for them, and what their body has told them no to in the past. She does not ask for medical records. She has an eye for the things medical records would tell her. If she declines to do a job she doesn't explain why; she says she's booked and she refunds whatever deposit was left.

**Hardware:** Clients can bring their own component — printed at a fabshop, sourced from a gray market supplier, pulled from a previous installation gone wrong — or buy from Thessaly's stock. Her stock is small and never advertised. Prices are negotiated in person. She will not install hardware she has not personally inspected and run a continuity check on. She has turned away approximately one in eight clients at this stage.

**SNT preparation:** Done the morning of the installation. The mixture ratio changes slightly based on the client's body mass, the installation site, and what Thessaly has learned from previous installations of the same component type. She keeps notes in a physical notebook that she encrypts in a personal shorthand. The notebook is also where she documents anomalies.

**Positioning and manacles:** The client lies down. Thessaly adjusts the table, marks the installation site, explains what will happen before each thing happens. The manacles close with a sound like a camera shutter. Most clients breathe differently after that — either slower, because they have decided to accept it, or faster, for the first thirty seconds, and then slower. She waits. She has never started an installation on someone who has not settled.

**Anesthesia:** Local, applied by hand, not by the rig. This is the only part of the process that Thessaly does herself with a needle. She uses a commercial dental block agent, which is not precisely correct for this application and is correct enough. General anesthesia is available for complex installations; it requires a second person in the room, a role usually filled by her neighbor Priya Olubunmi-Kessler, who is a retired Zone 3 emergency medical technician and who charges Thessaly in meals rather than money.

**The rig works:** Thessaly steps back from the table when the rig begins. She stands at the monitoring screens. The arms move with the specific quality of motion that very precise machines have — not smooth exactly, but without hesitation, each movement the shortest path between a start point and an end point, no wasted arc. The cutting is done. The threading begins: fine filaments of the component's neural interface array, guided through prepared channels in the tissue, aligned to nerve clusters that the design file specified and the rig's cameras confirmed. SNT is applied in sequence — each bonding point treated, held at pressure for the specified duration, checked by the camera optics before the rig moves to the next. The smell of burnt copper fills the back room.

Thessaly watches the screens. She talks when she talks. She is quiet when the work is fine.

**The handshake:** When the rig finishes, the component is physically installed. It is not yet integrated. The nervous system is aware that something has entered it and has opinions about this. The next twelve to seventy-two hours are the handshake period — the SNT bonds cure fully, the neural filaments seat into the tissue, the body decides whether the augment is something it can accommodate. Most rejections happen in this window. Thessaly sends clients home with a printed instruction sheet and her personal contact address — not a commercial channel, a personal one — with instructions to contact her at the first change in symptom character. She means this. She has gotten up at 3 AM for a handshake complication four times in the last year.

**Calibration:** Done on a return visit, two to five days post-installation, once the handshake has stabilized. Thessaly connects the augment to a calibration interface — a custom-built unit, not commercial — and runs the augment through its operational range while the client reports sensation. She adjusts the SNT threshold parameters remotely until the feedback loop is correct. Some augments take one session. Some take four. She does not charge for calibration sessions beyond the initial installation fee.

## What It Costs

Depends on the augment, the hardware source, and what Thessaly has learned about the client's situation from forty-five minutes of conversation at the counter. The range is wide. She has done installations for whatever a client could provide, when the client needed it and the augment was something she believed in. She does not advertise this. The neighborhood knows.

## The Community

Augments & Ink has been in the Rogers Park Gray Zone for six years. In that time Thessaly has done augmentation work on approximately 340 people and tattoo work on somewhere between 900 and 1,100 (she stopped counting tattoos after the first year). The neighborhood knows the shop in the way neighborhoods know things: by reputation, by word of mouth, by the fact that several people who live on the same block have gone through the curtain and come back functional. The shop is also where the block association posts notices, where certain informal disputes get arbitrated over the counter because Thessaly is considered level-headed, and where the block's children get their ears pierced at a rate that is not incidental to the shop's community standing.

The corponations know the shop exists in the way that corponations know things in Zone 3: as a data point in a risk assessment that has never cleared the threshold for action. Thessaly uses no corponation systems, has no registered business presence, generates no digital footprint that connects her legal identity to the shop. The shop's electrical draw is consistent with a tattoo parlor. The SNT tanks are unlabeled. The rig, disassembled, looks like salvaged industrial equipment.

The rig, assembled, is the most precise surgical instrument within twelve blocks.
